newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Decline in ozone layer picks up over Europe, US.
newsitem.headline: Decline in ozone layer picks up over Europe, US.

text.p: Europe and the United States were exposed in March to a bigger annual depletion of the earth's ozone layer, which shields against the sun's harmful ultraviolet rays, than in the same month of 1996, a U.N. agency said on Friday.

The World Meteorological Organisation (WMO) said the depletion, which occurs every spring in the northern hemisphere, was up to 15 percent over Western Europe, compared with 10 percent in March last year.
It was also much higher over the United States, between 10 and 15 percent compared to a decline of five percent a year ago.

Over the Arctic, the decline was between 15 and 25 percent and extended southward towards central Siberia, compared to an area covering Greenland and Western regions of Siberia last year, the WMO said in a statement.
The WMO blames chlorine and bromine released by man-made chemicals such as chloroflurocarbons (CFCs), which react with sunlight to destroy the ozone, for the decline.

The ozone is a fragile shield of gas that absorbs and blocks most ultraviolet rays of the sun. Scientists warn that skin cancers and cataracts could spread at alarming rates in the next few decades unless people protect themselves.
"People in Europe should have been careful during these weeks in March," said Rumen Bojkov, special adviser on ozone to the WMO.
"From Spain up to Denmark and Sweden and down to Italy, everywhere in central Europe was affected. People should not look at the sun in such days."
Bojkov says up to 10 percent of the ozone has been depleted over Europe and North America by man-made chemicals in the past 20 years.
The Bulgarian-born scientist has warned that the depletion will be even stronger within the next 10 years.
Studies show a one percent drop in ozone levels causes an average 1.3 percent rise in UB-V radiation.
